title: Galton board: many coin flips make a bell

bodies.name: Funnel
bodies.label: Funnel · releases the beads
bodies.describe: Every bead starts in the same place, above the first peg.

bodies.name: Copper bead
bodies.label: Copper bead · one random path
bodies.describe: Its bin is the number of times it bounced right. You can ride it (POV).

bodies.name: Pegs
bodies.label: Pegs · each one a coin flip
bodies.describe: At every peg a bead goes right with probability p, left otherwise.

bodies.name: Bins
bodies.label: Bins · the histogram
bodies.describe: Bin k collects the beads that bounced right k times.

bodies.name: Bell curve
bodies.label: Bell curve · binomial ≈ normal
bodies.describe: Printed on the glass: the normal curve with mean Np and spread √(Np(1−p)), scaled to the beads landed.

lessons.title: Ride one bead
lessons.question: Where will one bead land?
lessons.text: You ride the copper bead down the board. At every peg it bounces left or right, like a coin flip. Watch where it ends up.
lessons.explain: Its path was a string of 10 independent left/right choices, so each particular path has probability (1/2)^10 = 1/1024. The bin number counts only the right-bounces, and many different paths share a bin: C(10,k) of them end in bin k. One path leads to bin 0, 10 to bin 1, and 252 to bin 5. Where one bead lands is unpredictable. Where most beads land is not.
lessons.opens: What shape do many beads make?

lessons.title: Let the beads fall
lessons.question: What shape do many beads make?
lessons.text: Open the funnel wider (12 beads a second); the bins are emptied first. Watch them fill until 150 beads have landed, and compare the mean bin and the spread with the theory readouts.
lessons.explain: The count of right-bounces in N independent flips follows the binomial distribution: mean N·p = 5 bins, spread √(Np(1−p)) = 1.58 bins. After 150 beads the measured mean should sit within about 0.13 of 5 (the standard error 1.58/√150). The pile is already close to the gold normal curve: de Moivre–Laplace, the first central limit theorem (Le Cam 1986).
lessons.opens: What happens if the pegs favour one side?

lessons.title: Bias the pegs
lessons.question: What happens if the pegs favour one side?
lessons.text: Make right-bounces likelier (p = 0.75). The bins are emptied and refilled. Watch the pile build up to the right of centre until 150 beads have landed.
lessons.explain: With p = 0.75 the mean moves to N·p = 7.5 and the spread shrinks to √(10 × 0.75 × 0.25) = 1.37 bins. The pile is lopsided, with a longer tail towards the left: no bin above 10 exists to balance it. The normal curve fits less well when N·p(1−p) is small (here 1.9); a common rule of thumb asks for at least 5–10.

lessons.title: More rows
lessons.question: What do more rows do?
lessons.text: Add rows (N = 14) and set p back to 0.5. The board rebuilds with narrower bins. Watch the new bell grow until 150 beads have landed.
lessons.explain: With 14 flips the mean is 7 and the spread √(14 × 0.25) = 1.87 bins: wider than with 10 rows. But relative to the 14-bin range it is narrower: 1.87/14 = 0.13 against 1.58/10 = 0.16. Sums of many independent nudges spread out like √N while their range grows like N, so the bell sharpens relative to the board. That is the central limit theorem at work.
lessons.opens: How good is the normal curve for the centre bin?

lessons.title: Read the centre bin
lessons.question: How good is the normal curve for the centre bin?
lessons.text: Look closely at the bins near the middle and read the share of beads in bin N·p, with the binomial and normal predictions next to it.
lessons.explain: For N = 14 the exact binomial share of the centre bin is C(14,7)/2^14 = 3432/16384 = 20.9 %. The normal curve gives 1/√(2π·N·p(1−p)) = 21.3 %. With a few hundred beads the measured share still wobbles by about 2 percentage points around them (the standard error √(0.21 × 0.79 / n)); more beads shrink that wobble like 1/√n. The curve is an approximation that gets better as N grows (Galton 1889 built the board to show it).
lessons.opens: Why do sums of other independent random steps, not only coin flips, also make a bell?
